definition: Underwater computer vision is a subfield of computer vision.
details: In recent years, with the development of underwater vehicles ( ROV, AUV, gliders), the need to be able to record and process huge amounts of information has become increasingly important. Applications range from inspection of underwater structures for the offshore industry to the identification and counting of fishes for biological research. However, no matter how big the impact of this technology can be to industry and research, it still is in a very early stage of development compared to traditional computer vision. One reason for this is that, the moment the camera goes into the water, a whole new set of challenges appear. On one hand, cameras have to be made waterproof, marine corrosion deteriorates materials quickly and access and modifications to experimental setups are costly, both in time and resources. On the other hand, the physical properties of the water make light behave differently, changing the appearance of a same object with variations of depth, organic material, currents, temperature etc.

explainer.lead: Underwater computer vision is a subfield of computer vision focused on recording and processing information beneath water. It matters as underwater vehicles generate huge amounts of data that must be processed.

tiers.eli5: It's teaching computers to see clearly in murky water, so they can inspect structures or count fish.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply it to offshore inspection of underwater structures and to identifying and counting fish for biological research, often with ROVs, AUVs and gliders. A pitfall is that the field is still at a very early stage of development compared to traditional vision.
